title: Circulating Immune-Cell Profiles and Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis: A Community-Based Cross-Sectional Study
content:
Objectives: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) is associated with cardiometabolic abnormalities, but its circulating immune-cell profile remains poorly characterized. We examined associations of circulating immune-cell subsets and soluble inflammatory markers with prevalent DISH.
Method: This cross-sectional study analysed existing radiographic, clinical, and laboratory data from 526 participants in the Iwaki Health Promotion Project. Associations with prevalent DISH were examined using Firth penalized logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, and visceral fat area, with false-discovery-rate correction across the immune-cell and inflammatory-marker panel. Additional exploratory analyses evaluated relative and absolute CD16+CD56+ NK-cell measures, cardiometabolic adjustment, and radiographic phenotypes.
Results: Forty-one participants had DISH and 31 had early-phase DISH (EDISH). CD16+CD56+ NK-cell proportion was positively associated with DISH (OR 2.60 per 10-percentage-point increase, 95% CI 1.81–3.73), whereas CD16−CD56− proportion was inversely associated (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.29–0.58). Both associations remained significant after multiple-testing correction. CD4+CD8− helper T-cell proportion showed a nominal inverse association that did not survive correction. Absolute CD16+CD56+ NK-cell count was associated with DISH when modelled separately, but only the proportion remained statistically significant when both measures were included. Median proportions were 11%, 16%, and 18% in participants with neither DISH nor EDISH, EDISH, and definite DISH, respectively. No association with ossification burden was detected among participants with DISH.
Conclusions: DISH was associated with differences in circulating immune-cell proportions, most notably a higher CD16+CD56+ NK-cell proportion. These findings warrant independent confirmation and longitudinal investigation but do not establish a causal role for NK cells in spinal ossification.
